\section[en un principio]{en un principio — at first, in the beginning}

\label{lesson:ES-C535-en-un-principio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for next, then the Spanish for abruptly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: en un principio}
\textbf{en un principio} — \textquotedblleft{}at first, in the beginning\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
En un principio nadie creyó al niño.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{At first nobody believed the boy.}
\end{quote}

It often sets up a later change: \emph{En un principio..., pero luego...}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{en un principio} is built on \emph{principio}, which comes from Latin \emph{prīncipium} 'a beginning' (EtymDB), from \emph{prīnceps} 'first' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{en un principio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{en un principio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{en un principio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for next, then the Spanish for abruptly, then say \emph{en un principio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does en un principio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}At first, in the beginning\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a la larga]{a la larga — in the long run}

\label{lesson:ES-C535-a-la-larga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for abruptly, then the Spanish for at first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a la larga}
\textbf{a la larga} — \textquotedblleft{}in the long run\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A la larga, fue lo mejor para todos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In the long run, it was the best thing for everyone.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{a la larga} is built on \emph{largo} 'long', which is inherited from Latin \emph{largus} 'abundant, generous' (EtymDB). Spanish moved the sense from plenty to length.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a la larga}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a la larga}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a la larga}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for abruptly, then the Spanish for at first, then say \emph{a la larga} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a la larga mean? (\textquotedblleft{}In the long run\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tarde o temprano]{tarde o temprano — sooner or later}

\label{lesson:ES-C535-tarde-o-temprano}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for at first, then the Spanish for in the long run.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tarde o temprano}
\textbf{tarde o temprano} — \textquotedblleft{}sooner or later\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tarde o temprano vas a saber la verdad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Sooner or later you are going to find out the truth.}
\end{quote}

Spanish puts late first: \emph{tarde o temprano}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tarde o temprano} is built on \emph{tarde}, from Latin \emph{tardē} 'slowly, late', and \emph{temprano}, which is inherited from spoken Latin \emph{temporānus}, from \emph{temporāneus} 'timely' (EtymDB), built on \emph{tempus} 'time'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tarde o temprano}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tarde o temprano}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{tarde o temprano}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for at first, then the Spanish for in the long run, then say \emph{tarde o temprano} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does tarde o temprano mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Sooner or later\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[finalmente]{finalmente — finally, in the end}

\label{lesson:ES-C535-finalmente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for in the long run, then the Spanish for sooner or later.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: finalmente}
\textbf{finalmente} — \textquotedblleft{}finally, in the end\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Finalmente, la policía detuvo al ladrón.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Finally, the police arrested the thief.}
\end{quote}

Common in written stories and in the news.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{finalmente} is built on \emph{final} and the ending \emph{-mente}, from Latin \emph{mente} 'with a mind'. \emph{Final} comes from Latin \emph{fīnis} 'end' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{finalmente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{finalmente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{finalmente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for in the long run, then the Spanish for sooner or later, then say \emph{finalmente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does finalmente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Finally, in the end\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[más tarde]{más tarde — later}

\label{lesson:ES-C535-mas-tarde}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for sooner or later, then the Spanish for finally.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: más tarde}
\textbf{más tarde} — \textquotedblleft{}later\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Más tarde fuimos al hospital.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Later we went to the hospital.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Hasta más tarde} — see you later.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{más tarde} is built on \emph{tarde}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{tardē} 'slowly, late', from \emph{tardus} 'slow' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{más tarde}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{más tarde}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{más tarde}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for sooner or later, then the Spanish for finally, then say \emph{más tarde} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
